observations.content:
Summary: PEP 703, authored by Sam Gross and sponsored by Łukasz Langa, proposes to make the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) optional in CPython, allowing for a no-GIL build that produces a free-threaded interpreter. The PEP was accepted and finalized in October 2023, and it will be implemented in Python 3.13. The GIL will remain the default for standard CPython builds, but a new build configuration flag, --without-gil, will enable a free-threaded version. The sources indicate that work on the free-threaded path is ongoing, with Python 3.14 advancing it beyond the experimental stage, though full removal of the GIL depends on library compatibility and community adoption.

Summary: PEP 703 proposes adding a build configuration to CPython that makes the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) optional. This allows for a no-GIL CPython build, which is not ABI-compatible with the standard build due to changes to the Python object header. C-API extensions must be rebuilt for this version, and those relying on the GIL for thread safety will need additional explicit locking. The GIL is an obstacle to using multi-core CPUs efficiently, and making it optional aims to exploit CPU parallelism in more workloads. The Python Steering Council approved this PEP to help more scalable solutions to problems by removing the GIL barrier.

# What is PEP 703?

by Tim Hopper ·  Markdown

PEP 703: Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython is the proposal that makes a no-GIL CPython build real. It adds a build configuration that removes the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), the mutex that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, producing the free-threaded Python interpreter. [...] CPython gains a build flag, `--disable-gil`, that compiles an interpreter without the GIL. Because removing the lock changes the Python object header (to support biased reference counting), the free-threaded build is not ABI-compatible with the standard build. C extensions must be rebuilt, and wheels are published under a separate ABI tag carrying a `t` suffix.

    CPython builds without the GIL will not be ABI compatible with the standard CPython build or with the stable ABI due to changes to the Python object header needed to support biased reference counting. C-API extensions will need to be rebuilt specifically for this version.
 C-API extensions that rely on the GIL to protect global state or object state in C code will need additional explicit locking to remain thread-safe when run without the GIL. [...] The GIL is a CPython implementation detail that limits multithreaded parallelism, so it might seem unintuitive to think of it as a usability issue. However, library authors frequently care a great deal about performance and will design APIs that support working around the GIL. These workaround frequently lead to APIs that are more difficult to use. Consequently, users of these APIs may experience the GIL as a usability issue and not just a performance issue. ## Abstract

CPython’s global interpreter lock (“GIL”) prevents multiple threads from executing Python code at the same time. The GIL is an obstacle to using multi-core CPUs from Python efficiently. This PEP proposes adding a build configuration (`--disable-gil`) to CPython to let it run Python code without the global interpreter lock and with the necessary changes needed to make the interpreter thread-safe.

observations.content:
Summary: PEP 703 proposes making the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) optional in CPython, allowing for a build configuration that removes the GIL to enable free-threaded Python interpreters. This change aims to let multiple threads execute Python bytecode simultaneously, improving multi-core CPU efficiency. The proposal is currently in an experimental phase in Python 3.13, with plans for official support in Python 3.14. The Python community is testing this feature, and the Steering Council has emphasized a gradual rollout to minimize disruptions. However, some packages like SQLAlchemy may face challenges due to the potential performance impact on single-threaded programs and compatibility issues with concurrent applications.
